narration.full_text: Today, we're diving into one of the most foundational concepts in number theory: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. This theorem is incredibly powerful because it tells us something unique about every whole number greater than one. Simply put, it states that every composite number can be expressed as a product of prime numbers, and this factorization is unique, regardless of the order of the prime factors. For example, consider the number twelve. We can break it down into its prime factors: two times two times three. No matter how you arrange the multiplication, or what other prime numbers you try, you will always end up with two, two, and three as its prime building blocks. This uniqueness is what makes the theorem so fundamental. It's like every number has its own distinct prime fingerprint. Understanding this theorem is key to many areas of mathematics, including finding the HCF and LCM of numbers, which we've discussed previously.
